This phenomenon is increasingly recognized in insect physiology, where symbiotic microorganisms in the gut act as a biochemical shield, metabolizing or neutralizing xenobiotics before they reach their target sites (39, 40).

Comparative analysis of dose-response dynamics in R. ferrugineus adults and larvae under fed and starved conditions revealed that starvation signi ﬁ cantly increased the toxicity of insecticides, especially in larvae (39, 40, 44, 45).

Starved larvae showed signi ﬁ cantly lower LC 50 and LC 90 values for several insecticides (e.g., CORAGEN, FEDOTHRIN, and INDOCARB), indicating a reduced detoxi ﬁ cation capacity, probably due to a disturbed gut microbiota (40).
Exploiting starvation-induced physiological weakness may provide a complementary tool to chemical and biological methods for reducing palm losses (25, 26, 40).
